newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end down on rate hike nervousness.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end down on rate hike nervousness.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Tuesday as jitters about whether the Federal Reserve would or would not raise interest rates this month buffeted prices.

News of a 1.3 percent rise in the BTM/Schroders chain store sales index weakened the market early. Session lows were reached after a revised fourth-quarter productivity report was a little more bearish than expected. The government said productivity rose 1.1 percent, versus a 2.2 percent rise in the previous quarter. Unit labor costs, meanwhile, rose 2.5 percent, after rising 1.4 percent in the third quarter.

A news service report that Dallas Federal Reserve Bank President Robert McTeer told a luncheon gathering that the Fed was still on the fence with regard to raising interest rates briefly erased almost all the market's losses. McTeer was quoted as saying that there was "nothing to tip us over into tightening."

But Harvey Rosenblum, the Dallas Fed's research director, subsequently told Reuters that McTeer intended to emphasize the economic conditions of 1996, not to describe the stance of monetary policy in 1997.
The explanatory comments from the Dallas Fed, coming after a 1.1 percent gain in the Redbook survey of retail sales for the latest week allowed the market to weaken again.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 97-3/32, down 14/32. Its yield finished at 6.85 percent, versus 6.82 percent at Monday's close.
Traders said central bank and hedge fund selling weighed on the market early on.
But mainly the debate about how the Federal Reserve viewed monetary policy remained and prices were rangebound.

"Right now squarely in everybody's focus is (the Federal Open Market Committee monetary policy meeting on) March 25 and squarely in the rear view mirror is what the Fed Chairman has been saying -- the famous "irrational exuberance" remark," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc. "People want to believe the Fed isn't going to do anything on March 25, but they're not sure."
Hornbarger said the 30-year bond yield is squarely in a range between 6.50 percent and 6.90 percent.
"We hit 6.50 percent and bounced off of that pretty hard," he said. "We're closer to the top of the range now."
Hornbarger said he thought the market had priced in most of a potential 25-basis-point Fed rate tightening.

Allen Sinai, chief economist at Primark Decision Economics Inc., said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan "seemed to be in the business of 'risk management' in his recent Humphrey-Hawkins testimonies, laying the groundwork for a hike in the federal funds rate if deemed necessary, but not actually making clear that such a move was imminent. Sinai said since the latest round of price inflation indicators did not seem worrisome, the odds on any tightening at the FOMC meeting on March 25 appear less than 50 percent, "perhaps a 4-in-10 possibility."
Three-month bill rates ended down one basis point to 5.04 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.18 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.38 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 at 99-18/32, yielding 6.11 percent. Five-year notes were down 4/32 at 99-9/32, yielding 6.42 percent. Ten-year notes were down 8/32 to 97-19/32, yielding 6.58 percent.
